title: Pride, Class and the Cruel Little Irony
author: Lantern Editorial
summaryTr: Gerçekçi kısa öyküde gurur, sınıf ve ironi nasıl işler? Yazı, Maupassant'ın 'The Necklace' öyküsü üzerinden sıradan insanların trajedisini, anlatıcının suskunluğunu ve Çehov'la karşıtlığı inceliyor.
paragraphs: A borrowed necklace, a single glittering evening and ten years of drudgery: it sounds like the stuff of melodrama, and yet Guy de Maupassant's "The Necklace" (1884) is told with such restraint that its cruelty arrives almost without a sound. The narrator does not weep for Mathilde Loisel, nor does he scold her. He simply records, in a clear and measured voice, what happens when a woman who cannot afford to look wealthy decides that appearances are worth any price. Readers who have not yet read the story may wish to do so first, since this essay discusses its ending.

In a literary context, the word drama does not refer only to plays. In short fiction it denotes stories in which ordinary people face moral or emotional crises that are treated with complete seriousness, without the escapism of adventure or the exaggeration of horror. Such narratives owe a great deal to nineteenth-century realism, a movement that insisted that the lives of clerks, housewives and small tradesmen deserved the same attention that earlier literature had reserved for kings and heroes. Maupassant (1850 to 1893) was formed in this tradition. He learned his craft under Gustave Flaubert, whose insistence on the exact word and the impersonal narrator was to leave a lasting mark on his pupil.

The twentieth-century playwright Arthur Miller made a related argument in his essay "Tragedy and the Common Man" (1949). In his view, the ordinary person is as fit a subject for tragedy as any king, since what matters is not rank but the intensity with which an individual defends his sense of dignity. That perspective helps to explain why stories of this kind can feel weighty even though their settings are cramped apartments and office corridors.

In "The Necklace", class is less a fixed essence than a performance. Mathilde, the wife of a minor government clerk, feels that she was born for luxury and has been cheated by fate. When her husband obtains an invitation to a ministerial reception, she is miserable at having nothing suitable to wear, and so she borrows a diamond necklace from a wealthy friend. For one night the costume works: she is the prettiest woman at the party, admired and flattered. That success is exactly the problem. For a brief moment, social standing is revealed as a matter of clothing, jewellery and confidence, and the story invites us to wonder how much of rank is merely stage design.

O. Henry, writing in a very different register, treated money and status in a comparable way. In "The Gift of the Magi", poverty is not a moral failing but a constraint that shapes every choice the young couple makes. The comparison is instructive: Maupassant is severe with illusion, whereas O. Henry is tender about sacrifice, yet both authors understand that the economic pressures of urban life determine even the smallest decisions.
## Pride as the engine of plot

When Mathilde loses the necklace, she and her husband could simply confess to its owner and ask for time. Instead, they decide to conceal the loss, buy a replacement at a ruinous price and spend a decade paying off the debt. What drives this choice is not stupidity but pride: she cannot bear to appear careless, or poor, in front of someone she wished to impress. In the vocabulary of classical tragedy, pride is the flaw that turns an accident into a catastrophe, and in Maupassant's hands that flaw is entirely recognisable. We do not need to be Mathilde to understand why admitting a mistake can feel more dangerous than paying for it.

It is worth noting that pride has two faces in this story. The quality that ruins Mathilde also grants her a kind of dignity in the years that follow, when she learns the hardships of manual labour and faces her debt without complaint. The narrator remains ambiguous about whether this transformation is a punishment or an achievement, and one might argue that the emotional force of the story comes precisely from that uncertainty.

The final revelation, that the borrowed necklace was almost worthless, arrives in the last lines of the story, and Maupassant does not comment on it. There is no speech about fate, no moral summary. The irony is situational in the strictest sense: the sacrifice was made for something that never had the value attributed to it, so ten years of labour purchased what was, in effect, a copy of a copy. Because the narrator refuses to explain the reversal, the reader must confront its significance alone. This restraint is one of the hallmarks of realist short fiction, whose authors trust events, rather than editorial voices, to carry meaning.

The Russian writer Anton Chekhov (1860 to 1904) developed this restraint in a different direction. Where Maupassant tends to build towards a decisive turn, Chekhov often ended his stories without resolution, leaving characters at a moment of unfinished understanding. Comparing the two clarifies a basic choice in dramatic short fiction: whether an ending should deliver a verdict or merely pose an uncomfortable question.
## What the story still asks of us

Stories like these endure because they combine the particular with the universal. The details, a ball gown, a rented necklace, a clerk's salary, belong to nineteenth-century Paris, but the psychology they expose does not. In an age when a flattering public image has never been easier to produce, the temptation to pay almost any price to avoid looking diminished has hardly disappeared. The best dramatic fiction does not tell us what to feel about Mathilde. It presents her case with enough clarity that we are forced to decide whether we are judging her or ourselves.

quiz.q: What principle of nineteenth-century realism does the article emphasise?
options: Stories should always end with a moral lesson
Only people of high rank are suitable subjects for serious literature
The lives of ordinary people deserve the same serious attention once given to kings and heroes
Narrators should explain the meaning of events in detail
quiz.explainTr: Gerçekçilik, memurların, ev kadınlarının ve küçük esnafın hayatlarının da krallar ve kahramanlar kadar ciddi ilgiyi hak ettiğini savunur.

quiz.q: Why do Mathilde and her husband conceal the loss of the necklace?
options: Her pride makes her unable to bear appearing careless or poor
The owner has told them that she will not forgive the loss
They plan to sell the replacement for profit
They believe the necklace is worthless
quiz.explainTr: Karar budalalıktan değil gururdan kaynaklanır: Mathilde, özellikle etkilemek istediği birinin önünde dikkatsiz veya yoksul görünmeye katlanamaz.

quiz.q: What does the article mean by saying that pride 'has two faces' in the story?
options: It is admired by the narrator but condemned by the husband
It ruins Mathilde but also gives her a kind of dignity later on
It is shown in both the rich and the poor characters equally
It appears at the beginning and disappears by the end
quiz.explainTr: Mathilde'i mahveden aynı özellik, sonraki yıllarda ona bir tür onur da kazandırır; anlatıcı bunun ceza mı başarı mı olduğunu açık bırakır.

quiz.q: Why does the final revelation of the story have such force, according to the article?
options: A new character explains the moral at length
The narrator admits that Mathilde was wrong
Chekhov's influence makes the ending ambiguous and unresolved
The narrator offers no commentary and leaves the reader to face its significance
quiz.explainTr: Maupassant sonuç hakkında yorum yapmaz; anlatıcı açıklamayı reddettiği için okur sonucun anlamıyla tek başına yüzleşir.
